speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bennett for committee of supply and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Reid.
Mr. ERRICK F. WILLIS (Souris): Mr. Speaker, the debate on the amendment to

Grain Rates-Mr. Willis
go into supply has furnished the house with many important facts regarding freight rates in western Canada. In particular I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) upon placing on Hansard various freight schedules. It seems to me however that as the matter is now under appeal to the privy council, and as the Prime Minister has agreed that he will press the appeal as early as possible, the hon. member who has moved the amendment should withdraw it. I say the amendment should be withdrawn because it is of vital importance that this problem should not become a political football. Like other western members of the house I am interested in securing lower freight rates for western Canada. At the same time however I am also interested in securing a market for western barley. It is because of my interest in the market for barley that I have risen to my feet at this time. During the debate the statement has been made that the poultry men of British Columbia cannot use western barley because of the prohibitive freight rates. I say that such is not the case, nor is it the real reason. I make that statement because I have under my hand statistics to show that in the Fraser valley of British Columbia and in Vancouver barley can be purchased more cheaply than corn. Of course, in addition, those rates also apply to wheat. I say that the poultry men of British Columbia still have an opportunity of feeding barley instead of corn. The figures in this connection are these:
Prices of barley and corn for domestic use, Vancouver, May 18, 1931
Barley, No. 3 C.W., bulk, Vancouver and Fraser valley points, $20 per ton.
Corn, Argentine (No. 2 or better), bulk car-lots, Vancouver, $25 per ton; Fraser valley points, $27 per ton.
Corn, American, quotations delivery 10 days, Vancouver and Fraser valley points, $26 per ton.
These figures show that wherever corn is being fed in the province of British Columbia the poultry men of that province could save 20 per cent of their cost by feeding barley.

speechtext: The hens will not eat barley.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member has interrupted me by saying that the hens will not eat barley. The answer to that statement is that the agricultural experts of Canada are either experts or they are not. Through these experts experiments have been made in the provincial agricultural colleges of Canada, and through the Department of Agriculture for the Dominion which show that the two grains are practically inter-
22110- 116
changeable. That is to say, for poultry purposes barley may be fed as well as corn. I say these men either are experts or they are not. Their judgment,should be accepted or they should no longer be classed as experts of the Department of Agriculture. The argument may be used that the barley which is available in British Columbia is the product of that province. Such is not the case. In the year 1930 the province of British Columbia produced only 295,000 bushels of barley. In the province there are 22,800 farms whereon among other things, 64,700 swine are being fed. Hon. members will readily see that the supply of barley would last for only a few days. I am informed by the agent of the Dominion seed branch at Vancouver that the barley available in British Columbia is practically all western barley. Again, the seed branch of the Department of Agriculture is right or it is wrong. I say that the correct reason as to why the British Columbia poultrymen are not feeding western barley has not been given. If hon. members wished to go further in the matter of poultry feeding they might turn to pamphlet No. 128, new series, Department of Agriculture, which gives the general conclusion that barley is interchangeable with com. The statement has been made also that eastern Canada cannot feed barley because it is too dirty. May I bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that in Toronto the spread in price between barley and corn is 25 cents, and there are at the lake head at the present time 8,000,000 bushels of barley. If barley is dirty it can be cleaned for about 2 cents a bushel. It is available in Toronto for the use of poultrymen, swine feeders and live stock feeders at a saving of 23 cents a bushel as against corn. That is the saving which could be made by feeding barley instead of corn. During the last year there were brought into British Columbia 520,000 bushels of corn, the large part of which was fed to poultry. In my opinion, by a tariff that com should be made less available, and then they would have to feed western barley. The real reason behind the fact that the poultrymen of British Columbia do not feed barley is not a question of freight rates; the tree reason is that these men who feed corn will not change the diet of their pet hens. If we are going to work together in this country they must feed barley. The reason they are not doing so at this time is that they do not agree with conclusions arrived at by the Department of Agriculture. They do not believe the experts in that department, those experts who in the past have done so much to help them. That is the real reason, and I



Grain Rales-Mr. Campbell
say the time has arrived when the poultry-men of this country must come to the point of view of considering those Canadians in the middle west wljo are trying to make a livelihood by raising barley, rather than considering the dietetic eccentricities of any hen that ever laid eggs.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) made some statements with regard to export freight rates that I do not care to let go unchallenged. The hon. member expressed the opinion that export rates were, in effect, subsidized rates, that domestic business had to carry the whole burden not only of its own logical rates but the loss on export business. If this were so of course it would mean that the country as a whole is subsidizing export business. I do not agree with that view. It may be true of some commodity rates, but with respect to the particular rates that are under consideration-grain rates-I submit that the figures certainly prove the very opposite. I do not blame the hon. member or anyone else for holding such views, because the railway officials have for years past spent a great deal of time getting out propaganda to convince people that some of these commodity rates, such as the Crows-nest pass rates on grain, were a loss to the railway company. For instance, when testifying before the special railways committee in 1922, Mr. Beatty, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, predicted that if the Crowsnest pass rates were permitted to come into effect that year it would mean the Canadian Pacific Railway would fall short by $15,000,000 of paying its fixed charges and dividends. But what was the actual result? The Crowsnest pass rates did come into effect that year, and we find that the Canadian Pacific Railway, instead of being in the financial position predicted by Mr. Beatty, not only paid its fixed charges and dividends, but had a larger surplus than it had the previous year. Mr. D. B. Hanna, testifying for the Canadian National Railways, made a similar statement, and predicted that the operating deficit on the Canadian National system that year would be not less than $26,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was that with respect
to the whole system or just the western part?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The whole system. Of course, that was only the predicted operating deficit; he did not take into account the fixed charges. I find that that year, instead of the deficit being, as he predicted, $26,000,000, it was considerably less than in the previous year $15,000,000.

In this connection I might quote some figures published by the Canadian Pacific Railway with regard to their net earnings, which would seem to disprove the statement that the Crowsnest pass rates are losing rates to the railways. Let me take first the figures for 1924. In the first four months of that year, January, February, March and April, the net earnings on the Canadian Pacific system were a little over $5,000,000; for the second four months they rose to $9,000,000. Now, in those eight months there is a minimum of grain handled. But take the last four months, that is, September, October, November and December, the months in which the great bulk of the grain crop is handled, the months in which grain as a commodity furnishes a very much heavier percentage of the total traffic than it does in the other months of the year, and we find that for those four months the net earnings rose to the huge total of $22,000,000. Taking 1925, the net earnings for the first four months were $4,980,000; for the second four months $10,000,000; for the third four months -the very period in which according to the predictions made by these railway officials they ought to have had a heavy loss, the net earnings showed the enormous total of $26,000,000. Surely, sir, if these figures mean anything at all they mean that the grain crop handled under the Crowsnest pass rate is a profitable commodity to the railway. In 1923 I find that the total net earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway were $23,000,000, but the last four months accounted for $20,000,000 of the total, that is, the greater proportion was earned in the last four months. The Canadian National Railways show figures very similar. For 1924 the net revenue was $11,197,000, and almost all of this was earned in the four months in which grain was the largest part of the traffic.
Now let me take the operating ratio of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The operating ratio, I may explain, is the number of cents that a railway must spend to earn a dollar. In 1921, the last year in which the old grain rates were in effect, the operating ratio was 82.28; that is, the Canadian Pacific Railway had to spend 82.28 cents to earn a dollar. In 1922, the year that the Crowsnest pass rates came into effect, and the year in which Mr. Beatty had predicted the enormous loss to which I have referred, the operating ratio dropped to 80.55 cents; that is, it cost the Canadian Pacific Railway less to earn^ a dollar that year than it did in the preceding year.
In testifying before this same committee in 1922, Mr. D. B. Hanna stated that the

Grain Rates-Mr. Campbell
Canadian Northern Railway had always paid its way when it was operated as a western railway, and 1915, the year it was linked up with the eastern section, was the first year it has shown a loss. On the western section of the railway grain is by far the largest part of the traffic, and naturally if grain was handled at a loss the figures would be altogether different.
Let me take some further Canadian Pacific Railway figures as published by the company. These show that for the five-year period, from 1007 to 1011 inclusive, the system produced net earnings on the eastern section of $44,500,000, and on the western section $91,500,000. In the next five year period, 1912 to 1916 inclusive, the eastern section showed net earnings of $70,000,000 while the western section showed net earnings of $144,000,000. This again would certainly seem to indicate that grain is not handled at a loss.
Now I am going to touch another angle of this question. It seems to me that the passenger service is one of the services of both railways on which there is a heavy loss, and this ought to be given more consideration than has been given to it up to the present time. It is difficult usually to secure figures of the relative passenger and freight earnings. It is only when a rate case is being heard by the railway commission or by the courts that the railway companies produce figures that throw some light on this particular question. In 1922 the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway did produce such figures before the railway commission. Those figures showed that for that year the freight service on the Canadian National Railways produced a net operating surplus of $20,000,000, while the passenger service resulted in an operating deficit of $8,500,000. That, is, the railway company had to dip into the money earned by the carriage of grain, cattle, coal, lumber and other commodities, and take out $8,500,000 to pay the loss on the passenger service. In the same year even the Canadian Pacific Railway, efficiently managed though it may be and built as one unit from the very beginning, operating under the most favourable conditions, showed an operating deficit on the passenger service. These figures do not take into account at all the enormous investment in the passenger equipment of both railways. If these figures could be secured, they would show an enormous loss on the .part of the passenger services, and it seems to me something could be done and in fact something must be done to cut down the cost of passenger service.
I know people will complain when a train service is reduced, but the time has come
22X10-116i
when they will have to be allowed to complain. I think the duplication between the two great roads is almost a national disgrace. We have luxurious trains going across this continent every day; there are two of them leaving Winnipeg almost at the same time, and between Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal we find a tremendous amount of unnecessary duplication. Go through those trains to-day and you will find that in many cases not more than twentydive per cent of the space is occupied. It seems to me the time has come when the government will have to talk business not only with their own railway but to the Canadian Pacific Railway as well, and show them that there must be some reduction in the duplication of these services. In that way it seems to me some relief may be given in the matter of freight rates.
Let us consider the question of the Canadian National hotels, which are linked up with the passenger service. We are told it is necessary for the Canadian National Railways to spend millions of dollars in building hotels in order to hold the passenger gervice. If the passenger service is being carried on at a loss, why need we spend this money to bolster up that losing service? Look at the enormous amount of money which has been spent during the last few years by the Canadian National management. It is a national disgrace. Four million dollars was spent in Saskatoon, in my own province. Perhaps the hon. member for Saskatoon might not agree with me, but I say it was a totally unnecessary expenditure, even though it was spent in my own province. That is one of the things saddled on our freight service, with which we must deal one of these days in order properly to reduce freight rates.
But perhaps I am getting away from the subject matter of the resolution before the house. ^ The question of the disparity between domestic and export freight rates on grain is one that is exercising public opinion to a great extent in western Canada to-day, and it should be exercising opinion in eastern Canada as well, because after all the eastern farmer is paying the bill. While we are losing our market for a large quantity of our coarse grains, the eastern farmer is paying very much more than he should pay for his hog feed and chicken feed. There have been so many figures placed on the record during this debate already that I do not propose to cover the ground again, but I will just quote a few figures to show the extent to which this disparity exists. The. freight rate from Saskatoon to Liverpool to-day is about 62 cents per hundredweight on grain, while from Saska-
Grain Rates-Mr. Reid

toon, to Sherbrooke, Quebec, it is 70i cents. From Saskatoon to Truro, Nova Scotia, the rate is 74 cents; to Guelph, Ontario, it is 65i cents. Now take the figures via Vancouver. From Saskatoon to Liverpool via Vancouver and the Panama canal the average rate is 57 cents, but the export part of that rail rate is only 24 cents, whereas to ship grain to Langley, British Columbia, just a few miles from Vancouver, costs 50i cents.
This is a matter which, it seems to me, must engage the attention of parliament to some extent. Of course since it is now sub judice, so to speak, perhaps we are not in a position to deal with it here, but I do believe the debate has served a useful purpose in giving to the public information which they should have in connection with, this all-important question.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has pointed out that if I press the question to a vote it will defeat my object; in view of the fact that he has given the assurance that he is seized of the importance of the matter, and that as soon as possible it will receive attention, I ask permission of the house to withdraw the amendment. In doing so I assure hon. members that I brought this matter before the house in the utmost sincerity on behalf of the farmers of British Columbia.

speechtext:
By unanimous consent
leave is granted and the amendment is withdrawn.
Amendment withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I presume I will be in order now in discussing the main motion. As we are going into supply to discuss, among other things, the estimates of the Department of Marine, I wish to draw the attention of the house and the government to a matter of importance. I am sorry the Prime Minister is not in his place, because it was to him I particularly wished to address myself in pointing out the extent to which this department is lending itself to political jobbery.
I am not introducing an amendment to the resolution, expressing want of confidence in the government for the reason that this is largely a matter for the Prime Minister. He cannot be aware of the circumstances which I am going to mention. If after having heard them he takes appropriate aotion to cause justice to be done, then he is not deserving of a vote of want of confidence but rather a

vote of confidence. If on the other hand he ignores the situation and, by clever jugglery of words and phrases, proceeds to minimize it and to support the department in its action, then a vote of want of confidence which would be rejected by a majority of thirty would not particularly affect the situation. I would rather leave it in that way, in his hands, and if he does not see that the justice is done which the conditions as I will represent them, warrant, then the censure of his action will be rather in the form of loss of esteem by the people of Canada generally.
In an ordinary way I would say that the minister in charge of the department could not be held blameworthy, but in one of these cases to which I will more particularly refer, he is unmistakably to blame, because I informed him in writing of the whole circumstances and he never answered my letter, which was written more than a month ago. So far as I know he has done nothing to remedy the situation. I have not attempted to make political capital out of this matter, as I think will be proved by the correspondence I wall presently read; all I ask is that justice be done. As I say, under ordinary conditions, I would not be prepared to blame the minister; he is new to his position and it is generally admitted that he is in charge of a somewhat weak department. I am not here to take advantage of * my parliamentary immunity to slander men in any branch of the service, and I want to say emphatically that there are very many good men in that department who would be only too willing to make a success of their branches and bring the whole department to a creditable standard if they received the least encouragement, or if they even received permission, but it is a well known fact that for years the department has been run under a formula something like this: Change nothing; do nothing; stand still. Ignore the fact that Canada is growing, with ever increasing requirements of service, and above all block anything that savours of progress or of improvement.
That sounds like a strong statement; I wish I had more time and I would demonstrate it to the fullest degree. Take the case the other day, when the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) introduced a bill to amend a few of what he considered the grosser errors in the Canada Shipping Act. I see that the Province somewhat misquoted me by saying that I had expressed the opinion that the bill was obsolete. I was not referring to the hon. member's bill but to the whole act, and I might have added at the same time, with a

Marine Department-Mr. Neill
good deal of truth, that the whole department was obsolete. I am aware that the negotiations that have been going on in Britain for some time past-for the past two or three years or, at the outside, four-have somewhat precluded the idea of our revising the Canada Shipping Act at the present time. But that has been a matter of only two or three years. The fact is that the act has been rotten and obsolete for twenty years, yes, and thirty years. In 1908 or possibly 1911, I am not sure which, but over twenty years ago, somebody woke up in the department and drew up a complete revision of the act, and at that time, I believe, it was a wise and suitable one. I never heard any strenuous objections made to it. But they never got any further than that. That effort cost them so much exertion that they stood pat; and if any member came into the house full of fresh energy, and filled with a consciousness of the absurdity of our shipping act, and asked that action be taken, then the bill would be brought down from the shelf and dusted off, and they would show it as a proof of what they were prepared to do. Yes, they were prepared to do something. But the trouble is they never did anything. There was always some excuse: this man or the other was sick. It was always a case of "manana," as the Mexicans say. Literally it means "to-morrow", but the idiomatic significance of the word is that there are a whole lot of to-morrows-why, therefore, bother about to-day. Well, that is the spirit in which the act has been regarded during the last twenty years, and, as I say, it is still produced to-day to show what the department is prepared to do.
I can give many instances, much nearer the present time than that, to show where there have been neglect, evasion and failure to take action that has been vigorously called for. But what is the use of my wasting the limited time at my disposal? Those who have never had any business with the department are not interested, and to those who have had busines with them I do not need ' to state my case because my words find an echo in their own experience. It is possible that a strong, vigorous and determined man, taking hold of the department, might have reorganized it and made it a credit to the government of Canada. My hon. friend in charge of the department (Mr. Duranleau) sits opposite me, and, I admit, he presents all the appearances of having those characteristics of strength, vigour and determination. But unfortunately, so far as I have been able to find out, he has hitherto devoted all those energies only to making a strong,
vigorous machine of his department, instead of making a strong and vigorous department.
I will cite three cases, the last the worst of them, and I could go on much longer if time permitted. The first is the case of a man named Beattie, who was on a seasonal patrol job on the west coast for three years. I have here certain letters with reference to the matter but I shall read only the pertinent portions of them, for there is no use going into a lot of preliminaries. In November last I wrote to the agent as follows:
Beattie was on for three years running and did splendid work. Was on two years running at Pacheena. He is a returned man.
He applied this season.
Why was he rejected in favour of a nonreturned man?
This is the reply I received:
I regret that I am unable to reply to the query contained in this letter.
In desperation I then took the matter up with the minister himself, to whom I wrote: Dear Sir:	*
A man named Beattie acted as patrolman on the west coast for three years running, and did very good work, which was admitted by all who came in contact with him. He is a returned man.
He applied this season, as usual, and was rejected in favour of a non-returned man. Beattie took no part *whatever in politics.
Why was the preference given to a nonreturned man?
The reply I received from the minister three weeks later was as follows:
Dear Mr. Neill:
Replying to your letter of the 8 th April re Beattie, patrolman, west coast trail, I would point out that these positions are purely of a temporary and seasonal character. They do not continue from year to year, Last winter the Comox-Alberni men were taken from Bamfield.
To deal for a moment with the expression "non-permanent." The positions are non- permanent in that the work lasts only three months each year. But these men are classified, according to the Civil Service Commission, as "permanent seasonal." They are put on year after year. There must be thousands of men in all the departments who maintain their positions year in and year out, doing work regularly, re-appointed in a seasonal capacity. They are in that sense temporary, but it is not the custom to change them every year. If, however, that is to be the practice, how can you expect good service from men who know that their only requisite for employment is to stand in with the political powers of the moment? They know they will be fired the moment their party goes out. How, therefore, can they take an interest

Marine Department-Mr. Neill
in their work? Indeed, they may be fired at the end of the next year, and I submit you cannot expect good work under those circumstances. No reference whatever is made to the fact that this man, a returned man, who had given three years of good and faithful service, particularly good service, was let out and his place taken by a nom-soldier.
The next case is that of a man named Dean, from whom I have a letter and an affidavit. I will read the affidavit, which is explanatory.
What is the name?

0. S. Dean. The affidavit reads:
I	
do declare that in the month of May this year I applied to the coxswain of Bamfield life saving station for appointment to his winter crew. As he had a vacancy he told me I was accepted. I saw the coxswain after the election in September. He told me that if I wanted to go on the crew it would now be necessary to apply to a certain Mr. Braine. I did so, and Mr. Braine said I could not go on the crew on political grounds, that I was associated with the wrong party. I said, "you mean I voted wrong." "Yes! In fact feeling is so strong against the appointment of yourself that the coxswain will be fired if he takes you on."
I took no part in the recent Dominion election except to cast my vote. I am not a member of any political party. I am a war veteran and a reservist.
The affidavit is made in the prescribed form and is sworn to before a notary public. The letter is, of course, largely a repetition of the statements made in the affidavit, and I shall therefore read only that part of it that goes beyond the affidavit:
Next along came the election, of which I took little notice, and I went about my work .... According to the above scheme I am barred from .any government controlled job. I know this is not so, as the Premier of Canada said words to the effect that politics had not to interfere with the services, so that you can bring this specific case to the notice of the powers that be.
I am not writing to ask you to use your influence for me in any way but I am so annoyed at the extraordinary insulting position, that I want to expose the whole thing.
It will be seen that this man was not accused of being an active politician or anything of that kind, because he was not. He was only suspect, that is all. Had I been asked before or during or shortly after the election how the man had voted, I would have said with all sincerity that I did not know. That was the extent of my acquaintance with him or his possible political views. At any rate, it is not denied that he took no part in the election. Yet he, a returned man, was rejected in favour of a non-retumed man.

Now I come to the case of a man named Martin-Cameron, in connection with the life boat service at Tofino. It is the custom in connection with these boats to keep a permanent crew of six men, with an additional crew of four men in winter to look after wrecked vessels, boats that are lost, and so on. I have been familiar with the procedure for nine years and I know that the four winter men are selected by the coxswain. The only time I interfered was when I was approached by the Canadian Legion who accused the coxswain of not hiring a certain man who was a returned soldier. I asked the coxswain why he had not appointed this man and he said he was absolutely no good, and I have since found out that that was the case. I then told the Canadian Legion that they could recommend a man for the position as often as they liked and I would pass him on to the coxswain but there was one sine qua non for the appointment, and that was that the man, either soldier or non-soldier, had to be a capable seaman and pass the O.K. of the man in charge of the boat. I was not going to have on my conscience the responsibility of a shipwreck occurring a distance away, where valuable lives might be at stake, and the only means of help being a life boat -manned by politicians. I insisted that in every case the coxswain must pass finally on the application.
In this particular case a vacancy occurred a few months later and t'he coxswain put on the man recommended by the legion. He lasted only three weeks by which time he proved the bad opinion the coxswain had of him. It has since been discovered that even his claim to being a soldier was false. It happens occasionally that vacancies occur when men leave the permanent service. Late last fall one of the permanent men did leave and this man Martin-Cameron who had had three years' experience on the winter crew, who was a returned soldier and a highly educated man, suitable in every way for the position, applied for it, but a man named Evans was appointed. I wrote to the department in the following words:
I have your letter of this date advising me inter alia that V. Evans of Tofino is a member of the life boat at that place and that he was appointed October 11, 1930, permanently and that he is a returned man.
My information is very definite that he is not a returned man. Further, that Mr. Martin-Cameron a returned man and capable and experienced applied to you for the position and was rejected in favour of Mr. Evans, he not being a returned man but having political influence. I suggest you make strict inquiry into this.

Marine Department-Mr. Neill
I received the following reply:
I beg to advise that it has now been ascertained

After I stirred up the matter:
-that Evans is not a returned man. He was, however, properly recommended for the position and the appointment approved by the department.
Who recommended him?

Ah! The next is a letter
written a little later on by Mr. Martin-Cameron to myself, as follows:
I wrote to Mr. Graham (your late opponent), asked most politely if he would kindly explain how he came to recommend Evans when my application was in first and had three years' previous service besides being a returned man.
1 said I felt that as he had offered himself as a candidate for parliament he would not deliberately act against one who had voted for him and also against the laws of the country unless he had some reason I could not fathom.
And later on in the letter he states:
If any person obtains money under false pretences I believe it is a criminal offence against the laws of the country, and this is what Evans or his friends have done, so that I shall be glad and much obliged if you *null put my ease as I state it before the proper minister at Ottawa. Unless the minister is prepared to compound a felony he has only one course open, that is to cancel Evans' appointment and appoint me in his place.
When Mr. Martin-Cameron states that he voted for Mr. Graham, there are three reasons for my believing that that is the truth. First of all, before the election he said to a friend of mine that he was going to vote against me; after the election he told me quite frankly that he had voted against me, and, furthermore, I know the man and I know his type, and when he says that he voted against me, I believe him. In fulfilment of the request contained in Mr. Martin-Cameron's letter, I took the matter up with the proper minister, as I was in duty bound to do. I wrote to the minister under date of April 15, as follows:
In October last there was a vacancy on the permanent crew of the Clayoquot life boat.
Tofino is the same place. The letter continues :
Mr. T. Martin-Cameron, a local resident, applied for the position in the regular way. He is a returned man, and had the further qualification of having acted on the winter crew of the life boat for three years. I may explain that a small crew is kept on the year round as permanent employees, and in the winter time four extra men are taken on as temporary.
On the recommendation of Mr. Thomas Graham, defeated government candidate, a man named V. Evans was appointed. He was represented as being a returned man.
Mr. V. Evans is not a returned man. Therefore, the position was obtained by misrepresentation and should be cancelled and a
returned soldier, qualified by three years of experience, appointed in his place. Mr. Evans is probably still on probation.
These men are put on probation for six months and it would not be necessary to discharge this man, he could be told that he was not needed. My letter continues:
This is not a case of my trying to help a political supporter, because Mr. T. Martin-Cameron, I have every reason to believe, voted for my opponent; but it is a case of a qualified man wth years of experience, and a returned soldier, being turned down in favour of a man lacking these qualifications. I only ask that you should see justice done in the matter.
I was trying to shield the minister's reputation, and I put this matter up to him privately. I told him that if justice were done nothing would be heard of this matter. However, I did not receive an answer to that letter and, so far as I know, no action was taken. In due course I wrote to Mr. Martin-Cameron, as follows:
Rather than merely make political capital by explaining this matter in the house, which would not do you any particular good, I thought I would try to arrange it privately with the minister, and I wrote a letter to him, copy of which I enclose. You will see it is dated April 15th, and up to date I have received no answer. If that is to be the way, then the only alternative is to bring it up on the floor of the house and expose the deal, but if they would have agreed to do you justice I would not have said a word about it.
Mr. Martin-Cameron's reply reads as follows:
As you say, to have this matter brought up in the house might not do me personally any particular good, but I assure you my circumstances or feelings don't matter twopence as long as it helps in some way to stop or expose the political prostitution and abuse of patronage that seems so rampant in this province and possibly throughout the country.
Apparently he had written again to Mr. Graham, because he enclosed me a copy of the letter he received in reply. I would direct attention to one sentence in Mr. Graham's letter, reading as follows:
I see no reason why I should make any explanation re my actions.
That is the whole trouble with this system of political patronage-power without responsibility. Elections, yes and wars have been won on less popular slogans than that. What made the United States break away from the old country? It was taxation without representation, but is taxation without representation much worse than power without responsibility? I would not have dared to write such a letter to anyone because I am responsible to the people who sent me here. What happened in Comox-Alberni during the elections?

Marine Department-Mr. Neill
Did they elect two men, one to be a member and the other to ibe a tyrant; one man to represent them and the other to tyrannize over them? What is it but tyranny and oppression when the mass of the people have to be ordered and dictated to at the will of one man who acknowledges no responsibility and holds no mandate from the people whatever?
In another part of the district another instance occurred. A returned man, a Conservative all his life, had got a chance of getting a small job on relief work, but the secretary and the president of the local Conservative association laid their heads together and told the powers that be that this man was a Liberal, and one of the two recommended the other and he got the job. The returned man did not get it although he was a Conservative and was well known to be such when the matter was exposed. It is only an instance of the way these things are juggled with when you get power into the hands of irresponsible people, irresponsible in the sense of having no responsibility to the public. There is a body or party being got up in the province of British Columbia to try to do away with just such transactions. Among the evils of the party system which they list is this one:	'
Appointments are not made by the heads of departments but by the patronage committee, a group of supporters who know of nothing and care for nothing but the services the applicant has rendered to the party.
One of the planks in their platform of reform reads as follows:
To use every endeavour to destroy the party system for all time.
Then again we find the Province, a Conservative paper, saying editorially with reference to patronage:
The public is ill served by such a system. There is no stability in it. A man who does not know from year to year whether he is to go on in his job or not, merely at the will of a change of government, cannot be a really good citizen. He becomes a time-server and a pusillanimous fellow of little worth.
That is from the Province, and I say more power to them. Some of our newspapers make a practice of publishing in their daily issues news that appeared in newspapers one hundred years ago, and by a curious coincidence, almost on the date that this transaction I have mentioned occurred, this excerpt from the Observer, of September 26, 1830, was reprinted. The Observer was a well-known British paper, and I commend this excerpt to the consideration of the house:
The Duke of Newcastle has caused notices to be served on all his tenants who voted for

Mr. Serjeant Wilde at the late Newark election-not only those who gave plumpers against him, but those who gave half a vote only to his nominee. The number of persons who will thus be turned out of their houses, many of them perhaps born in them, amount to fifty-one.
In those days it was open voting, and they knew how people voted. To-day it is only hecessary to be a suspect. In those days they turned people out of their houses; today they turn them out of their jobs. 13 there much difference? Have we advanced very much in the last hundred years, after all? That is the curse of our public service. Is the government big enough to end it or is it only going to make excuses and pass it on? A gentleman on the opposite side of the house the other day said that if the government did not do something that he wanted done in his district, they were writing his political epitaph. The idea struck me that a suitable epitaph under these circumstances would be something like this. I would not apply it to the government. I would not say that it was appropriate to the department or to the minister, or even to an individual, but I would suggest that it should be put upon the grave of political patronage. I would suggest a cross of brass, the most brazen of our metals, and this inscription, which I am quite sure would be welcomed [DOT]by every well-thinking man and woman in Canada:
If heaven is pleased when sinners cease to sin,
If hell is pleased when rascals enter in,
If earth is pleased of grafters to be rid,
Then all, all are pleased, for-Patronage is dead.
So let it be.

There is something which I wish to draw to the attention of the house in connection with the expenditure of unemployment relief moneys in the province of New Brunswick. It will be remembered that last September I strongly opposed the placing under the supervision of provincial governments, especially the government of the province of New Brunswick, the expenditure of the unemployment relief grant that was voted at that session. I am not going to take up the time of the house to-day to repeat what I then said, but I wish to call attention of the hon. member who represents the Minister of Labour in this house to the manner in which this money has been spent in the province of New Brunswick under the supervision of the present provincial government.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Veniot
I shall not enter into any details of the political discrimination that was exercised in certain counties of the province of New Brunswick, beyond pointing out one or two facts which I am in a position at any time to' prove by the production of proper evidence. I wish, however, to call the attention of the house to an investigation that is now going on under a royal commission in the province of New Brunswick into the expenditure of provincial moneys under the Department of Public Works of the province. I refer more especially to the expenditure of moneys on roads and bridges. This investigation was asked for on the floor of the provincial legislature of New Brunswick last session, and a royal commissioner, the deputy attorney general, was appointed to investigate the charges. That investigation is now proceeding. Already five or six road supervisors have come before the commissioner and admitted their guilt in the padding of pay sheets. Some supervisors have admitted their guilt in that respect to the amount of thousands of dollars, others to lesser amounts. I find, Mr. Speaker, that of the five or six supervisors who have openly admitted their guilt, out of the sixteen or twenty who are to be brought before this royal commission, five are men who were employed as supervisors of roads to expend the money voted by this parliament for unemployment relief in the province of New Brunswick, under the supervision of the Department of Public Works of that province. The investigation that is now going on-I want to make this clear-does not touch the expenditure of the 120,000,000. It touches the expenditure of the revenues of the province on ordinary public works such as roads and bridges in the province of New Brunswick. But when I find that five or six supervisors have already admitted their guilt-
What have we got to do with that?

You have this to do with it. When I find that five or six supervisors who have already admitted their guilt before the royal commission now sitting in New Brunswick were the same men who were employed last fall and winter in supervising the expenditure of the moneys voted by this parliament for the relief of unemployment in New Brunswick, I think it is time that the Department of Labour took cognizance of the matter.
The other day I asked the hon. gentleman who represents the Minister of Labour whether the department received detailed
accounts from the Department of Public Works of the province of New Brunswick. He replied that the department did not, that they received merely a certificate issued by. the head of the department in the province, or by somebody connected with it, as to the proper expenditure of this money. If five or six supervisors have been guilty of padding pay sheets when they were spending the provincial moneys, there is every reason to suppose that they were equally guilty of padding pay sheets when they were expending money under the supervision of the provincial government, which had been voted by this parliament for the relief of unemployment in the province. However if that, is not sufficient to stir the Department of Labour to demand an investigation into the doings of the Department of Public Works in the province of New Brunswick, I am going to cite still another instance. I have in my possession a certified copy of a statement showing expenditures made on a certain bridge in my own county called the Connell bridge. The bridge is twelve miles from my own residence. The bridge superintendent was a defeated candidate in the provincial elections which took place in the province of New Brunswick on June 19, 1930. I find by the pay sheet in my hand that the superintendent of bridges is given credit for ten hours work per day at the rate of 60 cents an hour, while the workmen under him were working only eight hours a daj>'. If that is not padding a pay sheet, I want to know what it is. I have-

Let me give another instance or two. Up to within a year or two ago it was the practice of the Department of Public Works of New Brunswick to forward directly to individuals cheques for work performed by them. I do not know when the change took place whereby cheques were not sent directly to the individual, but were sent to'the supervisor for distribution to the workmen. What happened? In my own town and in my own parish men bad worked and earned money under the Unemployment Relief Act. Three days before Christmas the time for payment came and their cheques were sent for distribution to the two defeated candidates in the provincial elections.
Shame.

This was Dominion money. Those cheques were not distributed to the men on Christmas eve. At a public conference called in Bathurst to deal with the unemployment situation I asked one of these defeated candidates why the cheques were not distributed. He said they were held back because all the cheques had not come. Those men had to spend Christmas without a dollar to buy anything for their families. That is how the unemployment money was spent in my district. Let me go further.
We had better vote.

It is all right for the hon. member to interject, but let me say to him that while he may have had sufficient money in his pocket to buy his Christmas dinner those poor people had not one cent. Not only were the cheques held up by the defeated candidates but they were handed to merchants in the town of Bathurst to some of whom moneys were owing by the workmen. Money due two years back was kept out of their cheques, and their families were left without a cent.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
Were they postmasters?

They were not postmasters, and they were not ex-postmasters. In the lower end of the county of Gloucester some ex-postmasters may have been treated in that way since the present government has come into power. Their heads are being cut off right and left. Now, I wish to go one step , farther.
Fire another shot.

Let me go one step further. Let me relate another harrowing case. I cite the case of a man who was to receive $9.90 under the Unemployment Relief Act. He was a poor man and had only one arm. At home his wife and child were sick in bed. Although his cheque came, it went to the supervisor. The supervisor called him in and said, "Your cheque for S9.90 is here." The man replied, "I am glad to get it; you know about the state of affairs at my home; I am glad to get it." "No," the supervisor said, "you cannot get this cheque. You owe $14.35 to the agricultural society for two years and you will not get the cheque." That cheque he never got. They threatened to gaol him for the amount, and he had to go out and borrow the difference between $9.90 and $14.35 and pay it over to the supervisor. He had not a dollar left. Next day his wife and child were both dead ajid he had to borrow money to bury them. That is the way this money has been spent to relieve unemployment.
What did you ever do to relieve unemployment?
I never did anything like that. One thing is certain, if I did undertake to do anything for unemployment I would so surround it with safeguards that a poor man would not be robbed.
While you were in power you did not do anything.

No poor man ever came to my door to be turned away with a harsh word. I do not know whether I can say as much for the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. MeDade). He seems to be very much touched by the story I am relating. Right in his own county the cheques were never sent to the men who worked on the Tabusentac hill; they were sent to the supervisors and distributed among the merchants.
Not at all.
I make that statement and the hon. gentleman cannot deny it.
The human heart is touched.

I do not think there is any human heart at all in the distribution of this money. I am going to appeal to the acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) to obtain from the Department of Public Works of New Brunswick certified paysheets such as the one I hold in my hand, so that the matter may be looked into . I will give him the names on the paysheets I want, and I ask him to obtain those sheets. Further, when they are obtained I want a special investigation, based on the charges I make with respect to the paysheet I hold in my hand now. This is no hearsay. I know what I am talking about. Besides this paysheet showing this man working for ten hours a day at 60 cents an hour while the men only worked eight hours a day on the bridge according to the paysheet, that paysheet shows this superintendent employed for every day the men worked, and I can prove he was not on the work every day. Is that charge definite enough? Surely it ought to be. When I ask for an investigation I do not want any investigation held in the haphazard way that investigations are now being held in the province of New Brunswick. Into the charges I make I want an investigation held by a judge of a county or superior court, who can hear both sides and before whom we can have the parties represented by lawyers. I do not want the investigation held by a partisan commissioner. I make these charges and I am prepared to stand by them on the one condition-that a judge of a county or superior court shall be appointed to hold the investigation.

Mr. Speaker, had it not been for some of the references which have been made by my hon, friend the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) I would not have said a word to prolong the discussion, but I think it only fair on behalf of the Minister of Public Works in the Neiw Brunswick government and the other officials of his department who are and have been conducting the work, that something at least should be said in their defence. I am inclined to think, however, that it would have been advisable to have left the whole question in abeyance until some report had been received from the royal commission that is now making an investigation. Until that report is received by the people of New Brunswick I am thoroughly satisfied that it would have been much better to have left this question entirely alone. I would recall this to your mind, Mr. Speaker. In New Brunswick we have 1,300 supervisors of roads, and they are selected from men in every walk of life, in some cases men of very little education, and in some cases I doubt if we are able to get thoroughly honest men.

I wish to bring to the minister's attention certain recommendations that have been made by the Canadian Navigators' Federation. Would it be appropriate for me to bring this matter up on this particular item?

The Canadian Navigators'
Federation come to Ottawa every year and present their recommendations to the minister, and as a rule after they have made their recommendations and presented their petitions to the minister the house and the country never hear anything further of them. I must admit, however, that it is the opinion of the federation that this year they received the best hearing they have had in the existence of the federation. Their recommendations affect Shipping and the whole country so far as navigation is concerned,' although perhaps they may be more directly applicable to the great lakes.
First they ask that consideration should be given by the department to the load line for vessels on the great lakes. This is a very important matter. Many vessels have been lost with all hands owing to their being _ overloaded, more especially in the fall months of the year when ice forms freely on an already overloaded vessel.
I do not know whether the minister wishes to reply to each recommendation as I mention it or whether he would prefer that I give them all first and then let me have his opinion on them afterwards, but certainly I would like to have an expression of opinion from the minister as to these recommendations.
The second recommendation is that an inspection be made of all gas and diesel driven vessels over ten gross tons. They state that there are over three thousand of these vessels now on the great lakes, including lake Winnipeg, and as they are engaged in competition with steam driven vessels in carrying passengers, the federation ask that they be inspected and be required to carry lifesaving equipment. There is no inspection of these gas and diesel driven vessels at the present time as there is in the case of steam driven vessels, and to the layman it does look as though we had now reached the stage where an inspection of these boats is necessary.

doctor.

I have already corrected that statement once or twice in the house, and I wish to correct it again. I never made any such statement. I would like to make another correction. I did not say that I considered the Mafeking cut-off a part of the Hudson Bay railway.

In that case I shall have to read a report of a speech by the Minister of Railways at Dauphin, June 29, 1930, as follows:
"Mr. Bennett has promised to build the Mafeking cut-off."
Mr. Bennett does not consider the Mafeking cut-off a branch line of the Canadian National railways, but a part of the Hudson Bay railway system to be built by the Dominion government.
To build the Mafeking cut-off will not mean political interference with the Canadian National Railways. No public man has ever given a more solemn or emphatic pledge on any matter than has Air. Bennett that he will preserve the integrity of the Canadian National Railways.
That is the report of a meeting held at Dauphin on June 29, 1930, in which the Minister of Railways is quoting Mr. Bennett as saying that he did not consider the Mafeking cut-off a part of the Canadian National Railway system, but as part of the Hudson Bay railway and that it should be built by the Dominion government.

What is my hon. friend
quoting from?
From a statement that has been given to me of a report of a speech given by the minister.

Supply-Railways-Mafeking Cut-off

This is a matter of some importance. I may say for the 'benefit of hon. gentlemen who perhaps are not familiar with the railway situation in that part of the country that Mafeking is situated on a branch line of the Canadian National that runs up to Prince Albert. It is about twenty-five miles from the Saskatchewan boundary and about sevjenty miles from Hudson Bay Junction. For the people of Manitoba to get to Churchill they have to go to Hudson Bay Junction, and then, the road comes back at an angle of sixty degrees to The Pas. This Mafeking cut-off, which was promised' by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways, would form the third side of the triangle, and if we remember our mathematics aright, any two sides of a triangle are together greater than the third side. This cut-off would save probably seventy miles. There has been a strong demand in the province of Manitoba for a shorter line to Hudson bay than the present one, and the Mafeking out-off has been very strongly supported by some constituencies in Manitoba, those lying to the west, principally the constituencies of Nelson and Dauphin. This question formed one of the chief issues in the election campaign last summer in that part of Manitoba, and it can safely be said, I think, that the present member for Dauphin owes his election entirely to the promises that were made by the present leader of the government to build the Mafeking cut-off.
Where does the hon. gentleman get this report?
It was furnished to me. If it is not true, the minister can say so.

I did not make that
promise. I will speak as soon as my hon. friend is through.

I have said that the Mafeking cut-off formed one of the chief issues in the election in that part of the country. The former Minister of Railways, Hon. T. A. Crerar, speaking at a meeting in Dauphin, declined to give any such promise. He was questioned on the matter of the Mafeking cut-off and he came forward and made a straight statement.
More than he ever did in this house.

He made no promises that he knew he was not in a position to fulfil. I have been told by a number of people in that constituency that because the Hon. T. A.
Crerar did not make rash promises that he knew he could not carry out, Mr. Ward, the Liberal candidate, lost the election in that constituency.

quoted from a statement which is supposed to be a report of a speech of mine, would he mind quoting from a report of Mr. Crerar's speech?

I am just going to do that. The Hon. T. A. Crerar, speaking at Dauphin on July 19, 1930, said:
I am not here to tell you that the Mafeking cut-off 'null be built. The Mafeking cut-off is a branch line from one point to another on the Canadian National railways and is not a departmental matter. I cannot ask parliament to advance the money to build this road unless it is recommended by the directors of the Canadian National Railways. A study is being made of all phases, and if the directors of the Canadian National Railways recommend this construction I will give the matter consideration. From the standpoint of freight rates the Mafeking cut-off should not be built.
It is quite easy to understand, Mr. Chairman, that when a responsible minister of the crown, speaking in a constituency in which the Mafeking cut-off was perhaps one of the chief issues, comes forward with a plain statement of that kind, making no promises that he knew he could not fulfil, a large measure of support would be withdrawn from the government candidate and go to the men who made the promises.
Here is an extract from a poster that was used in the election of Mr. J. L. Bowman, the Conservative candidate in that constituency:
If you want the Mafeking cut-off, there is only one way to get it. Vote Bowman. Printed by the Dauphin Herald and Press. Dauphin, Manitoba, by the authority of J. N. McFadden, official agent for J. L. Bowman, Conservative candidate.

.... will see it through with all auxiliary *works and development necessary to its effective operation.



Supply-Railways-Mafeking Cut-off
The present Prime Minister at Brandon said:
The Mafeking cut-off is one of the works which should now be under way, not only as a needed public improvement but as a means of relieving unemployment.

As I have said, this was one of the chief issues in the constituency of Dauphin. I think the hon. member for Dauphin is in the position of a man who has been the recipient of goods obtained by false pretences.
Oh, oh.

From the standpoint of freight rates the Mafeking cut-off should not be built.
After the Hon. Mr. Crerar had made that speech it was felt that he had thrown cold water upon the campaign of the Liberal candidate in that constituency. The Minister of Railways has made the statement that the people of Dauphin chose the present member for the constituency rather than the former member because they considered the hon. gentleman a better man. Now I am not going to institute any comparison between the two gentlemen, for I have not heard anything to the detriment of either of them. But the Minister of Railways knows perfectly well that often it is not the personality of a candidate that determines the outcome of an election; it is the policies of the government or of the opposing party. And it was the policy of this government as enunciated by the present Prime Minister with reference to the Mafeking cut-off that determined the election in the constituency of Dauphin. The Hon. Mr. Crerar made a statement there and the Minister of Railways went at a later date and made another statement. These two statements were before

the people of Dauphin, and if the Hon. T. A. Crerar had made the same sort of speech as the minister has made to-night, there would have been no difference between the policies of the two parties. But it is well known, and the hon. member for Nelson has admitted it, that it was on the representations made by the present Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways in regard to this matter that the people of Dauphin made their choice as between the two candidates. The statement made by the Minister of Railways at that time was not a conditional promise. The people accepted it as unconditional, and, comparing it with the conditional statement made by the Hon. Mr. Crerar, they acted accordingly. I say, therefore, that the present member for Dauphin sits in this house because of the promise made in regard to the Mafeking cut-off by the present leader of the government and his Minister of Railways.
I might suggest that Mr. Crerar, the late Minister of Railways, was not accepted even in his own constituency.
That has nothing whatever to do with it.

He was beaten by 2,000 in a constituency that knew him well, so that they did not pay much attention to his promises of any kind. I followed him even in his own constituency and he was not very careful in his language. We knew him in this house. I sat with him in this house for a number of years and he was not any more particular with his promises than my hon. friend from Ldsgar-or myself-
Speak for yourself; don't speak for me.
He was not as good a politician as my hon. friend; the results show that. He was not thought very much of in his own constituency.
Camouflage.
At any rate, the results show that the people of Dauphin thought that Mr. Bowman and not his opponent should be here, and we shall have to stand by that for a while.

This is
a considerable item-86,000,000-for the Hudson Bay railway and terminal, and under it I presume I am at liberty to discuss the general railway situation. As this is probably the only opportunity I shall have for the purpose, I wish to refer the Minister of Railways to pledge No. 5 in the Prime Minister's famous Winnipeg speech. This reads:

We pledge ourselves to the improvement of the whole scheme of Canadian transportation northward by the completion of the Hudson Bay route, and the construction of such branches as may be necessary to render it most readily available to every part of Canada; to the Pacific slope by a Peace river outlet, and east and west by the development of the St. Lawrence waterways.
I had fondly hoped, Mr. Chairman, that there would be in the estimates some amount to implement that pledge given by the Prime Minister in his famous keynote Winnipeg speech in regard to the Peace River situation; and much as I am impressed by the representations made by hon. members from Manitoba with reference to the Hudson Bay route, I wish to impress upon this house the fact that, as a national asset to Canada, the development of the Peace River outlet is of far more consequence than the development of the Hudson Bay terminals, because there is no question in the world-
Be careful.

I am
being careful. I am going to support this item, but I wish at the same time to impress upon the house the fact I have just stated, that, as a national asset, the development of the Peace River outlet is of more importance than the construction of the Hudson Bay terminal upon which we are spending, according to the minister, the gigantic sum of $50,000,000, for a limited season ranging from twelve or thirteen weeks to a maximum of fifteen weeks a year.
Now, I do not want the Minister of Railways to come back with the statement that the late administration was in power nine years and did not carry through the Peace River outlet scheme. We have a new administration in power to-day, and the present Prime Minister's clearcut and explicit promise has been given with respect to the matter. He gave a specific promise in that pledge, No. 5, to proceed with the Peace River outlet. Let me point out to the minister that we are not dependent on the Pacific coast upon a landlocked port, open only three or four months of the year. In the city of Vancouver, at Prince Rupert and at Stewart in the far north we have three beautiful harbours, among the finest in the world, to any one of which this outlet could be constructed.
I do not wish to interrupt my hon. friend, because he is a delightful speaker. But I would point out to him that the Peace River outlet hardly comes under the Hudson Bay vote.

I am
coming to that.

I am not averse to discussing it, although it is now nearly eleven o'clock, but the hon. member is really out of order in dealing with the question under this vote.

My
only reason for bringing it up now is that, before I can support this item of $6,000,000, it is necessary that I should have a declaration of policy from the Minister of Railways in regard to that pledge given by his leader. I have read the pledge; it is No. 5. If the Minister of Railways is not prepared to unfold to parliament and the country the intentions of himself and of the administration in regard to the Peace River outlet, then I think it is incumbent upon this house to leave this item over until the Prime Minister is in his seat; because those of us, on both sides of the house, who have come from British Columbia, are absolutely pledged to work night and day for the construction of this Peace River outlet, which is a most vital question to us. And it is really not a political question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member really think it comes under this item?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I am discussing the relative merits of this vote of $6,000,000 and the Peace River outlet. An item can be discussed in two ways, either absolutely or relatively by comparing the proposal involved with other projects. I am discussing this item in the latter way.
The Minister of Railways came to the city of Vancouver and made speeches just as facile and voluble as the one he delivered in Dauphin on June 27, when he pledged himself to start the construction of this Mafe-king cut-off. However, his remarkable lucidity, facility and volubility of expression did not avail him very much.
You were there, that is the reason.

Ig the hon. minister now in a position, remembering the declaration of the Prime Minister during the special session that all these promises were to be implemented immediately, to inform the committee and the province of British Columbia, which is most vitally interested, what the policy of the administration is going to be, either now or in the near future, in regard to the construction of an outlet from the Peace River area to the Pacific ocean?

If my hon. friend will take this matter up on the railway estimates I will 22110-1191.
give him a statement. The matter of a Peace River outlet is being investigated by the two railways. I think my hon. friend heard me state in the house that a report had been made by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I have a copy in my office, although I have not the company's permission to table it, but when Mr. Beatty returns from England he and Sir Henry Thornton are to meet in my office early in June to discuss the whole question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This discussion is out of order, because speeches in committee must be directly relevant to the item under consideration.
It can serve as a notice of motion.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is within the knowledge of every hon. member who has sat in this house for any length of time that it is relevant to point out in regard to certain proposed expenditure that some other expenditure might have been undertaken somewhere else. Otherwise there would be no opportunity for an hon. member to complain that a certain work had not been undertaken in his own riding. Where would be the opportunity for an hon. member to ask questions with reference to a public work in, or affecting his constituency, not provided for in the estimates, unless in connection with an item covering a similar work in some other part of the country? I submit that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is perfectly in order.

The hon. member by
his remarks has confirmed me in my opinion. Ample opportunity is afforded to discuss any item which is submitted, and every reference must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration. Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
